beats.intro: Lesson eleven. [[sub]]What gets in the way of good decisions, and six questions that clear the path.
beats.emotions: The ideal model is hard to follow, because people bring emotions to every decision. [[list]]Pride, ambition, fear, insecurity. [[new]]They surface fastest when people who don't usually work together must decide together.
beats.roleplay: At Intel's very first management training session, a group of peers role-played a real problem from their jobs. [[out]]Their chairman, one level up, was sent out of the room. [[circle]]For about fifteen minutes they talked in circles, and none of them noticed. [[back]]The chairman came back, listened, frowned, and finally slapped the table: you are talking in circles. [[fast]]After that, the problem was solved in short order. [[name]]Grove called it peer-plus-one. Peers look for someone more senior to take charge, even if that person is not the expert.
beats.herd: Why? Most people are afraid to stick their necks out. [[john]]An Intel engineer described it like this: [[feel]]everyone feels each other out, waiting for a consensus before taking a position. [[weak]]Then someone offers it, weakly, as the group's view: I think our position seems to be. [[firm]]As others buy in, it gets restated more and more firmly. [[same]]In the car company, people waited for the boss. Here they wait for the group. Either way, nobody speaks their mind.
beats.confidence: The cure is self-confidence. [[fam]]Part of it comes from knowing the issue, and from experience. [[gut]]But mostly it comes from a gut-level understanding: nobody ever died from making a wrong business decision, or from being overruled. [[lead]]If a group stalls and has no chairman, the person with the most at stake should take charge. [[senior]]Failing that, ask the most senior person present. They may know less about the issue, but they act as a godfather of how decisions get made.
beats.fears: Two fears do the most damage. [[dumb]]The fear of sounding dumb. It stops senior people asking the questions they should, and makes others whisper to a neighbour instead of speaking up. [[each]]Every withheld fact or question makes the decision worse. [[over]]And the fear of being overruled in front of peers, which holds junior people back even more than fear of sanctions. [[unsure]]Sometimes people are honestly unsure. Experts say, we don't know what the company wants. Managers know they lack the technical detail. [[will]]Use intelligence and willpower anyway: start the discussion, and take a stand.
beats.timing: Sometimes discussion never produces a consensus, yet the time to decide has come. [[decide]]Then the senior person must decide. [[legit]]Using position power at that point is legitimate, even unavoidable. [[early]]Using it any earlier is destructive. [[nice]]Many managers hesitate, because giving orders feels not nice, and discussion drags on. [[criteria]]So don't push too early: wait until the real issues, not the early superficial ones, are on the table. [[late]]But don't wait too long either, or people drift away from a near-consensus that was close to right.
beats.six: A decision is an output, so say up front what output you expect. [[q]]Settle six questions in advance. [[w1]]What decision needs to be made? [[w2]]When must it be made? [[w3]]Who will decide? [[w4]]Who must be consulted first? [[w5]]Who will ratify or veto it? [[w6]]And who must be told?
beats.plant: Here is Grove's own example, the Philippine plant from lesson nine. [[what]]What: build a multistory plant next to the existing one, or a low building on cheaper land farther away. [[when]]When: the plant was needed in two to two and a half years, so working back with offsets, decide within a month. [[who]]Who decides: construction managers and plant managers at matching levels, two each, so both sides weigh in equally, each having consulted their own staff. [[ratify]]Who ratifies: Grove, the first boss they had in common. [[inform]]Who is told: Gordon Moore, the chairman. [[result]]The group chose to build next door, capped at four stories. Grove probed their facts and reasoning, and ratified it.
beats.veto: Why settle this in advance? [[late]]Imagine someone with veto power who only sees the decision at the end, and vetoes it. [[demor]]People who worked on it for weeks are demoralized, [[pol]]and even a sound veto looks like politics. Settling the six questions first prevents that. [[drama]]And if your final word is far from what people expected, announce it, but don't walk away. [[recon]]Adjourn, let people absorb it, then reconvene and hear their views.
beats.sloan: Good decision-making is hard, and always has been. [[sloan]]Alfred Sloan, who ran General Motors, warned that leaders are tempted to decide alone and skip the burdensome discussion. [[wayne]]Grove knew a manager with a John Wayne mentality who left Intel for a company where people decided on their own. [[back]]Four months later he was back. [[why]]If he could decide without consulting anyone, so could everyone else.
beats.wrap: To sum up. [[w1]]Peers often circle until someone senior steps in: the peer-plus-one. [[w2]]Fear of sounding dumb or being overruled withholds what the decision needs. [[w3]]The senior person decides only when discussion is done: not too early, not too late. [[w4]]Settle the six questions before you start. [[w5]]No surprise vetoes; if the answer shocks, reconvene. Now the lesson practice.
